title: Commit-window leasing and backfill-credit system for capacity-safe fleet rollovers
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Context: Recent Dedicated fleet rollouts have produced short, high-amplitude surges when pools are drained and testers/backfills compete with active traffic. Hard drains and single-shot evacuations cause autoscalers to overreact (scale-up then immediately scale-down), increasing cost and transient latency. Goal: implement a leasing + crediting model so the rollout controller can request time-bounded capacity leases from the autoscaler and be allocated backfill credits that allow controlled, metered use of ephemeral capacity during the upgrade window without causing autoscaler thrash.

What we propose: 'Commit-window leasing' is a lease the upgrade controller requests per GPU-slice or pool for a bounded time window (e.g., 30–90 minutes). Leases carry a target qps/core allocation and a 'backfill credit' budget measured in token-minutes used for temporary extra admissions (e.g., to accept queued KV-cache warmups, live drain bandwidth, or migration copies). The autoscaler, pool admission layer, and tenant admission controller will honor leases by: 1) reserving a soft slice of capacity from headroom calculations, 2) allowing backfill admissions until credit exhaustion, and 3) gracefully throttling new work if the cluster nears actual capacity.

Design notes and trade-offs: 1) Lease durations must be conservative to avoid starving production traffic; we use decreasing pro-rated windows for repeated attempts. 2) Credits are strictly accounting constructs that do not bypass safety checks — when utilization/cold-start risk passes thresholds the system switches to 'protect' mode and revokes backfill usage. 3) We avoid persistent cross-tenant credit carryover: credits are ephemeral and reconciled post-window to reduce long-term accounting complexity. 4) Autoscaler integration must remain declarative: the upgrade controller proposes a lease; the autoscaler can accept, accept-partial, or reject based on policy and current scaling behavior.

Implementation plan (high-level):
- Lease API: controller -> autoscaler endpoint with {pool_id, desired_headroom_tokens, window_seconds, reason}.
- Credit ledger: lightweight in-memory + periodic persisted reconciliation per-pool that records issued and consumed credits for observability.
- Admission hook: admission layer consumes credits for temporary admissions (warmup jobs, replica backfills).
- Soft-throttling policy: admission layer reduces acceptance rate proportionally to remaining credit and current utilization.
- Fallbacks: if lease rejected or revoked, upgrade controller falls back to conservative wave-based slow-drain and extended canary.

Acceptable success metrics:
- <5% increase in 95th percentile latency on affected routes during rollouts (measured token latency).
- <10% extra cost delta compared to non-upgrade baseline for the same period (measured as GPU-minutes and autoscaler churn).
- No tenant observed errors attributable to capacity eviction during the window.

Rollout & verification plan:
1) Feature flag behind controlled rollout.
2) Staging: integration tests with synthetic workloads to validate lease acceptance, partial acceptance, and rejection flows.
3) Canary: enable in 2 small pools (non-critical tenants) for one week with intensive telemetry.
4) Gradual expansion to 25% of pools with automatic rollback trigger on metric thresholds.
5) Full rollout once stabilized and SLOs met for 48 hours.

Runbook notes for oncall:
- If 'lease-revoked' alarms fire, pause active upgrade waves and run 'upgrade-hold' path.
- If credit exhaustion causes backpressure with rising error rates, trigger immediate upgrade rollback and notify capacity team.

Why different from prior work: Instead of increasing buffer slices or enlarging ephemeral pools, this ticket formalizes a time-bounded leasing handshake and metered backfill econ to reduce autoscaler thrash and provide predictable upgrade economics. This complements existing staged-rollout and transitive-evacuation controllers by providing an autoscaler-aware admission contract.
comments: 2026-02-16: Kickoff with Release Eng, Runtime and Autoscaler. Agreed to prototype a lease API and simple credit ledger before deeper admission integration. (Notes: Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/ENG-84719)

2026-02-22: Design review with capacity team. Decided lease window defaults: 30m for small pools, 90m for large pools. Jonas to spike a PoC of the ledger. Action: ENG spike branch created: https://github.com/redwood-inference/fleet-control/pull/3122

2026-02-28: PoC completed — basic lease accept/reject flow and an in-memory ledger. Observed autoscaler partial-accept behavior; need to add backpressure signaling. PoC logs: https://logs.redwood.ai/poctest/ENG-84719

2026-03-01: Integration tests running on staging. Discovered race where two concurrent upgrade controllers requested overlapping leases on same pool. Decided to add single-writer lock per-pool and optimistic retry in controller. Jonas to submit PR for lock.

2026-03-04: UX session with Product and Console teams to add visibility into active leases and credit burn rate in rollout timeline. Console card prototype: https://console.redwood.ai/rollouts/ENG-84719
2026-03-05: Code review opened for autoscaler-side accept/reject policy with simulated scenarios. Requested changes from Seema (Capacity) on partial acceptance heuristics.
acceptance_criteria: Lease API exists and is documented (controller and autoscaler contracts).
Credit ledger emits metrics for issued, consumed, and expired credits per pool.
Admission hook consumes credits and exercises soft-throttle when credits low.
Integration tests demonstrate autoscaler partial accept/reject and controller fallback behavior.
Canary rollout shows <5% P95 latency increase and autoscaler churn within budget.
